key_facts: **Mycosis fungoides (MF)** is the commonest cutaneous T-cell lymphoma: slowly evolving patches, plaques and sometimes tumours.
Patches in **sun-protected 'bathing trunk'** areas (buttocks, hips, breasts), varying shape, mild itch; often misdiagnosed as eczema or psoriasis for years.
Repeated biopsies (off steroids) with T-cell receptor gene studies may be needed.
Early stage: skin-directed therapy (potent steroids, phototherapy, radiotherapy); most have a normal life expectancy.
**Sézary syndrome**: erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, circulating malignant T cells: specialist.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **MF is the commonest primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL)**, about half of all primary cutaneous lymphomas. It is usually indolent over years to decades, with a minority progressing. **Sézary syndrome** is the leukaemic, erythrodermic variant.

sub: Adults 50–70; men twice as often; about 0.5 per 100,000 per year.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Clonal skin-homing CD4+ memory T-cells (CD4+, often CD7- and CD26-). Cause unknown; links to chronic antigen stimulation have been proposed. **Pautrier microabscesses** (intraepidermal collections of atypical lymphocytes) and **epidermotropism** without spongiosis are the histological hallmark, but they are absent in many early biopsies.

ul: **"Lymphoma always spreads quickly"**: early MF is indolent; most never progress.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: MF is a **clonal expansion of skin-homing CD4+ T cells** that infiltrate the epidermis.

mech.t: A clone of memory CD4+ T cells carries skin-homing receptors (CLA, CCR4).
Malignant cells invade the epidermis, forming Pautrier microabscesses.
Over years, deeper infiltration produces plaques and tumours.
mech.caption: Mycosis fungoides evolves from patch to plaque to tumour.

mech.t: Rarely, cells reach nodes and blood (advanced stage, Sézary).

histo: Atypical cerebriform lymphocytes in the epidermis (epidermotropism), Pautrier microabscesses; CD4+, loss of CD7; clonal TCR rearrangement.

ul: **Patch stage:** persistent, variably shaped, often **finely wrinkled ("cigarette-paper") pink-brown patches in sun-protected "bathing-trunk" sites** (buttocks, hips, breasts, inner thighs). Itchy or asymptomatic, **steroid-resistant or relapsing**.

**Erythroderma**, poikiloderma (atrophy, mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia), and variants (folliculotropic, hypopigmented in skin of colour and children, granulomatous slack skin, pagetoid reticulosis).
**Multiple biopsies** (ideally after a 2–4-week washout of topical steroids) with immunohistochemistry and **TCR gene rearrangement** (clonality). Diagnosis often takes years.

**ISCL/EORTC algorithm for early MF**. Diagnosis needs **≥4 points**: **Clinical:** 2 points for the basic criterion (persistent and/or progressive patches/plaques) plus 2 of the additional criteria (non-sun-exposed distribution; size or shape variation; poikiloderma), or 1 point for the basic criterion plus 1 additional; **Histopathology:** 2 points for a superficial lymphoid infiltrate plus both epidermotropism without spongiosis and lymphoid atypia, or 1 point for the infiltrate plus one of those; **Molecular:** clonal TCR rearrangement = 1 point; **Immunopathology:** CD2/3/5 <50% of T-cells, CD7 <10%, or epidermal/dermal discordance = 1 point

ul: Staging investigations (specialist): FBC + blood film/flow cytometry for Sézary cells, LDH, LFTs, HTLV-1 serology, and CT (or PET-CT) for stage ≥IIA or as indicated. Biopsy suspicious nodes.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: **Chronic eczema (including occupational contact dermatitis, relevant to a mechanic; patch test)**, psoriasis, tinea corporis (scrape), parapsoriasis (small- and large-plaque, where large-plaque can progress), pityriasis lichenoides, **drug-induced pseudolymphoma / MF-like drug eruptions** (reported with, among others, anticonvulsants, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, **amlodipine** and other calcium-channel blockers, and dupilumab-associated CTCL unmasking), lichen planus, cutaneous lupus.

ul: A **rash not responding to an appropriate potent topical steroid over several weeks, especially in sun-protected sites, should be referred for biopsy**. Do not repeat or escalate steroids indefinitely, as happened for 12 months in [Case 5](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma). Refer **routinely to urgently depending on stage clues** (tumours, erythroderma, lymphadenopathy, systemic symptoms: urgent). Primary cutaneous lymphoma is managed in **specialist supra-network skin lymphoma MDTs**.

Review drug triggers. Stopping a suspected culprit (e.g. amlodipine) and reviewing after 6–12 weeks may be appropriate *before or alongside* biopsy. This is a joint decision with the GP/dermatologist.

[Case 5](condition:basal-cell-carcinoma) medicines: **canagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor)** has no link to MF but carries genital mycotic infection and DKA risk (check the patient's wellbeing). Metformin: none. Simvastatin + amlodipine: the BNF/MHRA cap simvastatin at **20 mg** with amlodipine (CYP3A4 interaction), so check the dose.

**Early (IA–IIA): skin-directed therapy.** Potent/very potent topical steroid; **phototherapy** (narrowband UVB for patches, PUVA for thicker plaques; the course answer); topical **chlormethine gel** (Ledaga®); localised radiotherapy; topical bexarotene (not UK-licensed); and for many IA patients, "expectant" skin-directed care.

**Advanced (IIB–IV):** Total-skin electron beam therapy; Systemic **bexarotene** (hypertriglyceridaemia and central hypothyroidism; needs a lipid-lowering agent and levothyroxine; **avoid gemfibrozil**); Low-dose **methotrexate**; Interferon-α; **Mogamulizumab** (anti-CCR4; NICE TA754: Sézary after ≥1 systemic therapy, MF stage IIB+ after ≥2); **Brentuximab vedotin** for CD30+ (NICE TA577); Extracorporeal photopheresis (Sézary); Chemotherapy; Allogeneic stem-cell transplant in selected patients
Quality of life: **itch** (emollients, antihistamines, gabapentin/pregabalin, mirtazapine, aprepitant for refractory itch), and work and psychological impact.

Consider stopping a suspected culprit (e.g. amlodipine) and reviewing at 6–12 weeks, jointly with GP / dermatology.
Skin-directed: topical steroids, phototherapy; advanced disease: systemic therapy.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Dupilumab**: Biopsy atypical adult-onset ‘eczema’ before biologics: CTCL can be unmasked.

refer.t: Fixed patches or plaques in sun-protected sites failing treatment for months: biopsy.
**Erythroderma with lymph nodes**, intense itch, weight loss: **Sézary syndrome**.
Tumours or ulcerated nodules in known or suspected MF.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Fixed patches or plaques in sun-protected sites that fail to respond to treatment over months: refer for **biopsy** (MF).
Erythroderma with lymph nodes, intense itch and weight loss: **urgent** referral (Sézary syndrome).
Stage IA: normal life expectancy; advanced stages much poorer.

pearls: Explain that early MF is usually a **chronic, indolent** condition (stage IA has near-normal life expectancy). Avoid the "advanced cancer" framing without staging.
Cumulative UV raises skin cancer risk.
**Dupilumab caveat:** CTCL has been unmasked or accelerated in patients misdiagnosed with atopic dermatitis. In an atypical adult-onset "eczema" that is failing treatment, biopsy before biologics.

quiz.a: Multiple biopsies after a 2–4-week steroid washout.

quiz.q: Why biopsy before dupilumab in atypical adult eczema?
quiz.a: CTCL can be unmasked or accelerated.
